ety.text: Proto-Slavic *ǫpyrьder. Serbo-Croatian vampirbor. German Vampirbor. French vampirebor. English vampire From French vampire, from German Vampir, via Hungarian from a Slavic word, probably Serbo-Croatian vàmpīr /ва̀мпӣр, from Proto-Slavic *ǫpyrь, further possibly from Proto-Turkic *ōpur (“glutton, witch, evil spirit”), or from native construction. Doublet of dhampir and oupire.

senses.d: A mythological creature (usually humanoid and undead) said to feed on the blood or life energy of the living.
ex: Bram Stoker's novel Dracula built on centuries-old stories of vampires and also encouraged new growth of the mythology.
The universal belief is, that a person sucked by a vampyre becomes a vampyre himself, and sucks in his turn.

senses.d: A person with habits traditionally ascribed to (literal) vampires, such as heliophobia, being a night owl, having pale skin, and so on.
ex: Somehow I doubt that Kelly will want to go surfing with us — she's such a vampire that she might recoil from the sun, lol!

senses.d: A person with the medical condition porphyria cutanea tarda, colloquially known as vampirism, with effects such as photosensitivity and brownish-red stained teeth.
A blood-sucking bat; vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus)
A person who drains one's time, energy, money, etc.
ex: You have to be careful what you tell her, because she's such a vampire for drama.

senses.d: A vamp: a seductive woman who exploits men.
A medical technician who works with patients' blood; especially, a phlebotomist.
Synonym of anti-ship missile (ASM), particularly an incoming hostile one.
To drain of energy or resources.
